title: Files & Object Storage
subtitle: Follow a 2 GB video upload straight into an object store, and see why your API server never touches the bytes.
learn: How block, file, and object storage differ and which fits which job
Why big files go in an object store and their metadata in a database
How a presigned URL lets a client upload without passing through your API
How multipart upload makes huge uploads resumable and parallel
How a CDN serves reads and how an upload event triggers background work

steps.title: Where do the bytes go?
steps.body: A user taps Upload on a 2 GB video. Your app also needs to remember who owns it, its title, and whether it has been processed yet. Do you push 2 GB through your API servers into a database column? Almost nobody does. This lesson shows where the bytes live, where the facts about them live, and how the two get connected.
steps.idea: Big binary data and small structured facts want different homes.
steps.caption: A client holds a 2 GB file, and the system must store it safely.

steps.title: Block, file, object
steps.body: There are three kinds of storage. Block storage is a raw disk: fixed-size blocks you read and write at an offset, used for database files and VM disks. File storage adds folders and paths that many machines can share (NFS-style). Object storage, like S3, is a flat bucket of whole objects found by key. You write a whole object with PUT and read it with GET, optionally just a byte range. You cannot edit bytes in the middle; you replace the whole object. In return you get huge scale, low cost per GB, and very high durability (S3 advertises 11 nines).
steps.idea: Block is for databases and VMs, file is for shared folders, object is for blobs at scale.
steps.caption: The object store holds whole blobs addressed by key.

steps.title: The naive path: proxy it
steps.body: The simplest design is to proxy: the client sends the file to the API, and the API forwards it to the object store. It works, but every upload ties up an API connection for the whole transfer, and each byte crosses the API's network twice (in from the client, out to the store). The metric shows 2,048 MB through the API for one file. With 2 GB per upload and ten thousand users, your API fleet moves 20 TB. A slow phone on bad Wi-Fi can hold a worker for minutes.
steps.idea: Proxying uploads turns your API into a bandwidth pipe, which is the wrong thing to scale.
steps.caption: Every byte passes through the API server on its way to the store.

steps.title: Metadata DB + blob
steps.body: Split the job in two. The blob (the raw file bytes) lives in the object store under a key such as videos/u42/9f3a.mp4. A row in the metadata database records the facts: owner, title, size, content type, the object key, and a status like pending. In the animation the client asks to upload and the API inserts that pending row. The database can answer 'list my videos by date', which an object store cannot do well, since it only lists keys by prefix. The row is the index; the blob is the payload.
steps.idea: Store the key and facts in a database; store the bytes in the object store.
steps.caption: The client asks to upload, and the API records a pending row.

steps.title: Presigned URL
steps.body: The API asks its storage library to sign a URL for exactly one operation: PUT this key, valid for 15 minutes. Signing is local math using a secret the client never sees, so it takes microseconds and needs no storage call. The client gets the URL and uploads straight to the store, so 0 MB pass through the API. Anyone holding the URL can use it until it expires, so keep lifetimes short and scope it to one key. A signed PUT does not limit size, so validate after upload or use a presigned POST policy with a size limit.
steps.idea: A presigned URL is a short-lived permission slip: the API grants it, the store honors it.
steps.caption: The API hands the client a signed, expiring upload URL.

steps.title: Upload in parts
steps.body: One 2 GB PUT is fragile: if the connection drops at 95 percent, you start over. So for big files the API starts a multipart upload and signs one URL per part (here 32 parts of 64 MB; S3 needs at least 5 MiB per part except the last). The client PUTs the parts straight to the store in parallel and collects an ETag (a receipt) for each. It sends the ETag list to the API, which calls complete, and the store stitches the parts into one object. A failed part is retried alone. Save the upload ID in the row so a restarted client can resume.
steps.idea: Multipart makes big uploads parallel and resumable: retry a part, not the file.
steps.caption: The API signs 32 part URLs, and the client uploads the parts straight to the store.

steps.title: React to the upload
steps.body: When the object appears, the store emits an event (for example ObjectCreated) to a queue or function trigger, and a worker picks it up. The worker reads the object and treats it as untrusted: it checks type and size, makes thumbnails or transcodes, then flips the row from pending to ready. If the worker crashes, the message is redelivered. Delivery is at-least-once, so processing must be safe to run twice. New S3 objects are strongly consistent, so the worker sees the file right away.
steps.idea: Use storage events to trigger background work, then flip the row to ready.
steps.caption: The object arrives, an event fires, and a worker marks the row ready.

steps.title: Serve it from the edge
steps.body: To watch the video, the client asks the API where it is. The API looks up the row in the metadata DB and returns a CDN URL. A CDN (content delivery network) keeps cached copies at edge locations near viewers. The first viewer in a region causes a cache miss, and the CDN pulls the file from the object store. Later viewers get the cached copy from nearby. Private files use a presigned GET URL straight from the store, or CDN-signed URLs if you still want edge caching.
steps.idea: Read through a CDN for speed and cost; use a presigned GET for private files.
steps.caption: The CDN fills from the store on a miss, then serves nearby viewers.

steps.title: The upload is abandoned
steps.body: The user closes the app after 20 of 32 parts. Those parts sit in the store, invisible but billed, and the row is stuck on pending. Two cleanups fix this. A job deletes pending rows older than a day and aborts their multipart upload. A lifecycle rule (a storage setting that acts on objects by age) aborts incomplete multipart uploads after, say, 7 days, as a backstop for anything the job misses. The mirror problem is deleting a row but forgetting the blob, so deletes should remove both.
steps.idea: Two systems mean two cleanups: expire stale multipart parts and stale pending rows.
steps.caption: A dropped upload leaves orphaned parts behind and a row stuck on pending.

steps.title: The whole pattern
steps.body: Bytes go in an object store, facts go in a metadata database, and the API only brokers permission. A presigned URL lets the client upload directly, multipart makes huge files resumable, events trigger processing, and a CDN serves reads. Block storage stays for databases and VM disks. Object stores cannot edit in place, so changing a file means writing a new object.
steps.idea: Keep your API out of the data path: sign a URL and let the client talk to the store.
steps.caption: The API handles tiny messages while the store handles gigabytes.

quiz.q: Why do most designs hand the client a presigned URL instead of proxying the upload through the API?
options: Object stores refuse requests that come from API servers
Presigned URLs encrypt the file in transit, which an API server cannot do
The bytes skip your API, so it only handles tiny requests and scales independently of upload volume
Presigned URLs remove the need for a metadata database
quiz.why: The signature is created locally and the client sends bytes directly to the store, so API servers do not carry upload bandwidth. You still need a database for metadata.

quiz.q: A 2 GB multipart upload of 32 parts fails on part 27 because of a network blip. What should the client do?
options: Retry only part 27, then complete the upload
Delete the metadata row and ask the user to try again later
quiz.why: Each part is uploaded and acknowledged independently with its own ETag, so only the failed part needs to be resent before the complete call.

quiz.q: Why store the object key and attributes in a database row rather than relying on the bucket alone?
options: Object stores cannot attach any metadata to an object at all
Object keys are not allowed to contain a user's name or ID
Objects are encrypted at rest so they cannot be read back by key
A database can query by owner, date or status; a bucket mainly lists keys by prefix
quiz.why: Object stores are good at get-by-key and prefix listing. Questions like all videos owned by user 42 this week belong in a database that can index those fields.

quiz.q: You need to update a single 4 KB page in the middle of a large data file many times per second. Which storage fits best?
options: Object storage, rewriting the object each time
Block storage, which supports reads and writes at an offset
File storage, because it stores folders of objects
A presigned URL with a long lifetime
quiz.why: Block storage allows small in-place writes at an offset, which is why databases use it. Objects are replaced whole, so a 4 KB edit would mean rewriting the entire object.

cheatsheet.def: Raw fixed-size blocks read or written at an offset. Used for database files and VM disks. Low latency, in-place updates.
Hierarchical folders and paths, often shared by many machines over a network. Good for shared home directories and legacy apps.
Flat bucket of whole objects found by key. Cheap, huge, durable, but no in-place partial edits: replace the whole object.
Keep owner, size, status and the object key in a database row; keep the bytes in the object store. The row is how you search and list.
A time-limited URL signed by your server for one operation on one key. Lets a client talk directly to the store. Keep expiry short.

Split a large file into parts (S3: 5 MiB to 5 GiB each, max 10,000). The API starts the upload and signs one URL per part; the client uploads in parallel, retries failed parts, then the API completes. Abort stale ones with a lifecycle rule.
The store emits a notification when an object is created, so a worker can scan, resize or transcode it. Handlers must be idempotent.
Cache popular objects at edge locations. Cuts latency and egress cost; for private content use a presigned GET from the store, or CDN-signed URLs to keep edge caching.
